claims.claim: A large cohort of axon collaterals from genioglossus premotor neurons projected to the motoneurons innervating the jaw-opening digastric muscle (anterior portion), which are located in the accessory trigeminal motor nucleus (Dig).
claims.source: Very interestingly, from the genioglossus transsynaptic tracing experiments, we observed that a large cohort of axon collaterals from these tongue-protruder premotor neurons projected to the motoneurons innervating the jaw-opening digastric muscle (anterior portion), which are located in the accessory trigeminal motor nucleus (Dig) medial and ventral to the main MoV (Figure 4E, arrow).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Many genioglossus premotor axons were observed projecting into the central MoVII, but not other divisions of MoVII, on both sides of the brainstem.
claims.source: Furthermore, many genioglossus premotor axons were observed projecting into the central MoVII, but not other divisions of MoVII, on both sides of the brainstem (Figure 4C, arrow; Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the imaging data shown in Figures 4C and 5C.

claims.claim: GFP+ boutons from genioglossus premotor neurons directly contact ChAT+ motoneurons in both the central MoVII and the Dig.
claims.source: Using high-resolution confocal microscopy, we observed GFP+ boutons directly contacting ChAT+ motoneurons in both the central MoVII (Figure 5C,D) and the Dig (Figure 5A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Subsets of genioglossus premotor neurons simultaneously provide inputs to digastric and/or platysma/lower lip motoneurons.
claims.source: These findings confirm that subsets of genioglossus premotor neurons simultaneously provide inputs to digastric and/or platysma/lower lip motoneurons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the anatomical data showing axon collaterals and boutons.

claims.claim: Tongue protrusion always involves concomitant opening of the jaw and movement of the lower lip.
claims.source: Considering many previous experimental observations of the co-activation of these muscles (Gerstner and Goldberg, 1991; Liu et al., 1993; Travers et al., 1997; Thexton et al., 1998; Naganuma et al., 2001), for example tongue protrusion always involves concomitant opening of the jaw and movement of the lower lip, such specifically shared premotor neurons are the simplest mechanism to generate co-activation of their target motoneurons.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observed phenomenon supported by citations.

claims.claim: Specifically shared premotor neurons are the simplest mechanism to generate co-activation of their target motoneurons.
claims.source: Considering many previous experimental observations of the co-activation of these muscles (Gerstner and Goldberg, 1991; Liu et al., 1993; Travers et al., 1997; Thexton et al., 1998; Naganuma et al., 2001), for example tongue protrusion always involves concomitant opening of the jaw and movement of the lower lip, such specifically shared premotor neurons are the simplest mechanism to generate co-activation of their target motoneurons.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the anatomical data.

claims.claim: Previous studies using retrograde tracers discovered the existence of neurons which project to both MoV and MoXII nuclei.
claims.source: Previous studies using retrograde tracers discovered the existence of neurons which project to both MoV and MoXII nuclei (Amri et al., 1990; Li et al., 1993; Travers et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The masseter exhibits some degree of synchronous activity with tongue-retractor muscles during feeding behavior.
claims.source: The masseter exhibits some degree of synchronous activity with tongue-retractor muscles during feeding behavior (Kakizaki et al., 2002), although they are not as tightly coordinated as the digastric and genioglossus muscles.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Tongue-retractor motoneurons are located in the dorsal MoXII, as compared to tongue-protruder genioglossus motoneurons which are located in the ventral MoXII.
claims.source: Tongue-retractor motoneurons are located in the dorsal MoXII, as compared to tongue-protruder genioglossus motoneurons which are located in the ventral MoXII (McClung and Goldberg, 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: A few masseter premotor axons specifically innervated dorsal MoXII and formed boutons opposing both contralateral and ipsilateral motoneurons located in this region.
claims.source: We found that indeed a few masseter premotor axons specifically innervated dorsal MoXII (Figure 5E,G), and formed boutons opposing both contralateral and ipsilateral motoneurons located in this region (Figure 5F,H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claims.claim: Shared premotor neurons innervating both jaw-closing and some tongue-retracting motoneurons could facilitate the co-activation of these two muscles.
claims.source: Thus, shared premotor neurons innervating both jaw-closing and some tongue-retracting motoneurons could indeed facilitate the co-activation of these two muscles.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the anatomical data.

claims.claim: Masseter and genioglossus motoneurons receive distinct sensory-related inputs.
claims.source: From the circuit-tracing results described above, it is immediately apparent that masseter and genioglossus motoneurons receive distinct sensory-related inputs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of the tracing data from the two muscles.

claims.claim: The masseter neurons receive extensive MesV-derived proprioceptive and SpVo-derived somatosensory inputs.
claims.source: The masseter neurons receive extensive MesV-derived proprioceptive and SpVo-derived somatosensory inputs, and the genioglossus neurons primarily receive SpVc-derived somatosensory inputs (compare Figure 2D,F with Figure 4A,F), while both motoneuron populations receive sensory-related input from dPrV.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of tracing data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claims.claim: The genioglossus neurons primarily receive SpVc-derived somatosensory inputs.
claims.source: The masseter neurons receive extensive MesV-derived proprioceptive and SpVo-derived somatosensory inputs, and the genioglossus neurons primarily receive SpVc-derived somatosensory inputs (compare Figure 2D,F with Figure 4A,F), while both motoneuron populations receive sensory-related input from dPrV.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of tracing data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claims.claim: Both masseter and genioglossus motoneuron populations receive sensory-related input from dPrV.
claims.source: The masseter neurons receive extensive MesV-derived proprioceptive and SpVo-derived somatosensory inputs, and the genioglossus neurons primarily receive SpVc-derived somatosensory inputs (compare Figure 2D,F with Figure 4A,F), while both motoneuron populations receive sensory-related input from dPrV.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of tracing data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claims.claim: Genioglossus motoneurons receive taste-related inputs from the NTS, while no labeling in the NTS was observed in the masseter premotor circuit.
claims.source: Additionally, genioglossus motoneurons receive taste-related inputs from the NTS (Figure 4B, inset), while no labeling in the NTS was observed in the masseter premotor circuit.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of tracing data from the two muscles.

claims.claim: In the rostral reticular formation where many of the premotor neurons for both muscles are located, these populations are distributed in a similar pattern, suggestive of spatial intermingling of these two groups of premotor neurons.
claims.source: However, in the rostral reticular formation where many of the premotor neurons for both muscles are located, these populations are distributed in a similar pattern, suggestive of spatial intermingling of these two groups of premotor neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the tracing data.

claims.claim: In the caudal-most IRt at the level of MoXII, masseter premotor neurons are situated ventrally to the labeled genioglossus premotor neurons.
claims.source: In the caudal-most IRt at the level of MoXII, masseter premotor neurons are situated ventrally to the labeled genioglossus premotor neurons (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dual-color tracing data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: At the level just rostral to the MoXII, sparsely labeled masseter premotor neurons are spatially intermixed with densely labeled genioglossus premotor neurons in the IRt.
claims.source: At the level just rostral to the MoXII, sparsely labeled masseter premotor neurons are spatially intermixed with densely labeled genioglossus premotor neurons in the IRt (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dual-color tracing data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: At the level of the MoVII and MoV, there is extensive spatial overlap between the two populations of premotor neurons in the reticular region (IRt and PCRt), and in regions surrounding MoV.
claims.source: At the level of the MoVII and MoV, there is extensive spatial overlap between the two populations of premotor neurons in the reticular region (IRt and PCRt, Figure 6C), and in regions surrounding MoV (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dual-color tracing data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claims.claim: The reticular regions with extensive spatial overlap between masseter and genioglossus premotor neurons have previously been found to contain central pattern generating circuitry for jaw and tongue movements.
claims.source: Notably, these regions in the reticular formation have previously been found to contain central pattern generating circuitry for jaw and tongue movements (Chandler and Tal, 1986; Lund, 1991; Nakamura and Katakura, 1995; Morquette et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Even when the premotor pools were intermixed, no double-labeled neurons were observed.
claims.source: However, even when the premotor pools were intermixed, we never observed double-labeled neurons; they remain distinct populations, avoiding simultaneous activation of these two muscles which could result in biting of one's own tongue.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the dual-color tracing experiments.

claims.claim: The absence of double-labeled neurons avoids simultaneous activation of masseter and genioglossus muscles which could result in biting of one's own tongue.
claims.source: However, even when the premotor pools were intermixed, we never observed double-labeled neurons; they remain distinct populations, avoiding simultaneous activation of these two muscles which could result in biting of one's own tongue.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the anatomical observation.

claims.claim: The majority of the masseter and the genioglossus premotor neurons are located in the intermediate reticular region (IRt) between the level of MoXII and the rostral end of MoV.
claims.source: The majority of the masseter and the genioglossus premotor neurons are located in the intermediate reticular region (IRt) between the level of MoXII and the rostral end of MoV.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative data from Tables 1 and 2.

claims.claim: The rostral portion of the IRt region between the inferior olive and MoV is thought to contain CPGs for jaw and tongue movements.
claims.source: Because the rostral portion of this region between the inferior olive and MoV is thought to contain CPGs for jaw and tongue movements (Chandler and Tal, 1986; Lund, 1991; Nakamura and Katakura, 1995; Morquette et al., 2012), we wanted to determine the potential output signs of labeled premotor neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Both the masseter and genioglossus premotor neurons in IRt are of mixed transmitter phenotypes (either excitatory vGluT2+, or inhibitory GAD1/2+ or GlyT2+).
claims.source: We found that both the masseter and genioglossus premotor neurons in IRt are of mixed transmitter phenotypes, that is they can be either excitatory (vGluT2+), or inhibitory (GAD1/2+ or GlyT2+) (Figure 7A–H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7A-H.

claims.claim: Premotor neurons in most brainstem regions are of mixed transmitter phenotypes.
claims.source: These mixed phenotypes are also true for premotor neurons in most other regions in brainstem (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is stated based on additional data not shown.

claims.claim: Only vGluT2+ neurons were detected in the cerebellar DCN and the midbrain dMRf, with a notable absence of GAD1/2+ or GlyT2+ neurons in these regions.
claims.source: However, in all samples examined, we only detected vGluT2+ neurons in the cerebellar DCN and the midbrain dMRf (Figure 7I–L), with a notable absence of GAD1/2+ or GlyT2+ neurons in these regions (data not shown) suggesting that the descending inputs from cerebellum and midbrain to jaw and tongue motoneurons are primarily excitatory.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7I-L.

claims.claim: The descending inputs from cerebellum and midbrain to jaw and tongue motoneurons are primarily excitatory.
claims.source: However, in all samples examined, we only detected vGluT2+ neurons in the cerebellar DCN and the midbrain dMRf (Figure 7I–L), with a notable absence of GAD1/2+ or GlyT2+ neurons in these regions (data not shown) suggesting that the descending inputs from cerebellum and midbrain to jaw and tongue motoneurons are primarily excitatory.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the neurotransmitter phenotype data.

claims.claim: Some premotor neurons traced from one muscle also form synaptic boutons onto distinct motoneurons located in different motor nuclei.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that in both cases, some premotor neurons traced from one muscle also form synaptic boutons onto distinct motoneurons located in different motor nuclei.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings shown in Figures 4, 5.

claims.claim: The mandible is connected by ligaments at the midline.
claims.source: Because the mammalian mandible is connected by ligaments at the midline, the output of left and right jaw motoneurons must be temporally symmetric.
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical fact.

claims.claim: When humans chew more on one side, the contralateral masseter is simultaneously activated to a comparable extent.
claims.source: Even when humans chew more on one side, the contralateral masseter is simultaneously activated to a comparable extent (Moore, 1993; Peyron et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Studies investigating the rhythm-generating properties of the brainstem after midline transection have found that sufficient circuitry exists on both sides of the brainstem to independently generate a rhythmic output.
claims.source: Studies investigating the rhythm-generating properties of the brainstem after midline transection have supported this theory through the finding that sufficient circuitry exists on both sides of the brainstem to independently generate a rhythmic output (Chandler and Tal, 1986; Ihara et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Previous studies have implicated commissural interneurons located inside MoV and bilaterally projecting neurons extending axons to both left and right MoV as a potential source of bilaterally coordinated inputs.
claims.source: Previous studies have implicated commissural interneurons located inside MoV and bilaterally projecting neurons extending axons to both left and right MoV in some brainstem regions as a potential source of bilaterally coordinated inputs (Appenteng and Girdlestone, 1987; Ter Horst et al., 1990; Juch et al., 1993; Kamogawa et al., 1994; Yoshida et al., 2005; McDavid et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Axon terminals of premotor neurons transsynaptically labeled from left masseter motoneurons extensively innervate the contralateral (right) MoV and form boutons opposing motoneurons.
claims.source: Furthermore, we observed axon terminals of premotor neurons transsynaptically labeled from left masseter motoneurons extensively innervating the contralateral (right) MoV (Figure 6C) and forming boutons opposing motoneurons (Figure 3G,H), supporting the existence of large numbers of bilaterally projecting premotor neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 3G,H and 6C.

claims.claim: The jaw premotor circuit includes the simplest configuration for bilateral coordination: a single premotor neuron that synapses on equivalent ipsilateral and contralateral motoneurons.
claims.source: It thus appears that the jaw premotor circuit includes the simplest configuration for bilateral coordination: a single premotor neuron that synapses on equivalent ipsilateral and contralateral motoneurons.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the anatomical data.

claims.claim: Bilaterally projecting premotor neurons are especially prevalent in the reticular formation region previously identified as containing the jaw CPG.
claims.source: Interestingly, these neurons are especially prevalent in the reticular formation region previously identified as containing the jaw CPG (Chandler and Tal, 1986; Chandler et al., 1990; Lund, 1991; Nakamura and Katakura, 1995; Morquette et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the dual-color tracing data combined with citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Tongue activity is tightly coordinated with jaw and facial muscle activity during feeding behaviors in a variety of mammals, including humans.
claims.source: Tongue activity is tightly coordinated with jaw and facial muscle activity during feeding behaviors in a variety of mammals, including humans (Westneat and Hall, 1992; Takada et al., 1996; Ishiwata et al., 2000; Yamamura et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The tongue-protruding genioglossus is active in phase with the jaw-opening digastric muscle and with the orbicularis oris of the lips under a wide range of conditions.
claims.source: More specifically, the tongue-protruding genioglossus is active in phase with the jaw-opening digastric muscle and with the orbicularis oris of the lips under a wide range of conditions (Liu et al., 1993; Takada et al., 1996), and the tongue-retracting styloglossus is often active in phase with the jaw-closing masseter muscle (Kakizaki et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The tongue-retracting styloglossus is often active in phase with the jaw-closing masseter muscle.
claims.source: More specifically, the tongue-protruding genioglossus is active in phase with the jaw-opening digastric muscle and with the orbicularis oris of the lips under a wide range of conditions (Liu et al., 1993; Takada et al., 1996), and the tongue-retracting styloglossus is often active in phase with the jaw-closing masseter muscle (Kakizaki et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Previous work studying body muscle coordination in vertebrates and invertebrates showed that distinct CPGs which control motoneurons of different body segments may interact with each other to effect cross-muscle coordination.
claims.source: Previous work studying body muscle coordination in vertebrates and invertebrates showed that distinct CPGs which control motoneurons of different body segments may interact with each other to effect cross-muscle coordination (Cang and Friesen, 2002; Briggman and Kristan, 2008; Smarandache-Wellmann et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Axon collaterals from labeled genioglossus premotor neurons also innervate MoV motoneurons supplying the jaw-opening anterior digastric muscles, as well as the motoneurons located in the central part of the MoVII.
claims.source: Our study discovered that axon collaterals from labeled genioglossus premotor neurons also innervate MoV motoneurons supplying the jaw-opening anterior digastric muscles, as well as the motoneurons located in the central part of the MoVII.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: The central MoVII supplies the posterior digastric muscle (jaw-opening and swallowing), the platysma muscle (which depresses the jaw and draws down the lower lip), and the lower lip muscle.
claims.source: The central MoVII supplies the posterior digastric muscle (jaw-opening and swallowing), the platysma muscle (which depresses the jaw and draws down the lower lip), and the lower lip muscle (Munro, 1974; Ashwell, 1982; Hinrichsen and Watson, 1984), which are all activated when the tongue is protruding (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Muscles supplied by central MoVII (posterior digastric, platysma, and lower lip) are all activated when the tongue is protruding.
claims.source: The central MoVII supplies the posterior digastric muscle (jaw-opening and swallowing), the platysma muscle (which depresses the jaw and draws down the lower lip), and the lower lip muscle (Munro, 1974; Ashwell, 1982; Hinrichsen and Watson, 1984), which are all activated when the tongue is protruding (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observed phenomenon with reference to Figure 5.

claims.claim: Axon collaterals from labeled masseter premotor neurons also innervate motoneurons located in the dorsal MoXII, previously shown to innervate tongue-retractor muscles.
claims.source: Additionally, we found that axon collaterals from labeled masseter premotor neurons also innervate motoneurons located in the dorsal MoXII, previously shown to innervate tongue-retractor muscles (McClung and Goldberg, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings shown in Figure 5E-H with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Specific premotor neurons simultaneously innervating multiple different groups of motoneurons provides the simplest circuit mechanism for enabling orofacial muscle co-activation.
claims.source: Our results indicate that specific premotor neurons simultaneously innervating multiple different groups of motoneurons provides the simplest circuit mechanism for enabling orofacial muscle co-activation (Figure 8B2).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the anatomical data.

claims.claim: It is likely that such common premotor neurons are located in IRt because the majority of labeled jaw or tongue premotor neurons are located in that region.
claims.source: It is likely that such common premotor neurons are located in IRt because the majority of labeled jaw or tongue premotor neurons are located in that region.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative distribution data.

claims.claim: During chewing, the tongue-protruding genioglossus and jaw-closing masseter are generally active with the same rhythm but in opposite phases to prevent biting of the tongue.
claims.source: During chewing, the tongue-protruding genioglossus and jaw-closing masseter are generally active with the same rhythm but in opposite phases to prevent biting of the tongue.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observed phenomenon with a functional explanation.

claims.claim: Many premotor neurons for genioglossus and masseter are located in a spatially intermixed pattern, especially those situated between the caudal end of MoVII and the rostral end of MoV.
claims.source: Here, we found that many premotor neurons for these two antagonist motor groups are located in a spatially intermixed pattern (especially those situated between the caudal end of MoVII and the rostral end of MoV) (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by dual-color tracing data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The region between the caudal end of MoVII and the rostral end of MoV is within the region proposed to contain the CPG for chewing.
claims.source: As this region is within the region proposed to contain the CPG for chewing (Chandler and Tal, 1986; Nozaki et al., 1986; Ihara et al., 2013), our findings suggest that premotor neurons for different orofacial muscles are embedded within the same rhythm-generating network.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Premotor neurons for different orofacial muscles are embedded within the same rhythm-generating network.
claims.source: As this region is within the region proposed to contain the CPG for chewing (Chandler and Tal, 1986; Nozaki et al., 1986; Ihara et al., 2013), our findings suggest that premotor neurons for different orofacial muscles are embedded within the same rhythm-generating network.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical data and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Previous studies examining intracellular potentials have found that masseter motoneurons receive rhythmic inhibitory and excitatory signals.
claims.source: Furthermore, previous studies examining intracellular potentials have found that masseter motoneurons receive rhythmic inhibitory and excitatory signals (Goldberg et al., 1982), while genioglossus motoneurons receive only rhythmic excitatory signals (Sahara et al., 1988).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Genioglossus motoneurons receive only rhythmic excitatory signals.
claims.source: Furthermore, previous studies examining intracellular potentials have found that masseter motoneurons receive rhythmic inhibitory and excitatory signals (Goldberg et al., 1982), while genioglossus motoneurons receive only rhythmic excitatory signals (Sahara et al., 1988).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In the reticular region previously implicated in rhythm generation, premotor neurons consisted of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
claims.source: In the reticular region previously implicated in rhythm generation, we found that premotor neurons consisted of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The NTS is thought to play a major role in taste processing.
claims.source: The NTS (nucleus of the solitary tract) is thought to play a major role in taste processing (Bradley and Grabauskas, 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Previous tracing studies have suggested that the NTS contains neurons which project directly to the hypoglossal nucleus.
claims.source: Previous tracing studies have suggested that the NTS contains neurons which project directly to the hypoglossal nucleus (Aldes, 1980; Borke et al., 1983; Travers and Norgren, 1983; Dobbins and Feldman, 1995; Ugolini, 1995; Fay and Norgren, 1997).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Some NTS neurons provide monosynaptic input onto tongue-protruding genioglossus motoneurons.
claims.source: Our results support these findings, revealing that some NTS neurons provide monosynaptic input onto tongue-protruding genioglossus motoneurons (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the tracing data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The taste reactivity test has been used extensively in assessing the interaction of taste processing and ingestive behaviors.
claims.source: While sparse, this input could play a central role in the well-established taste reactivity test (Grill and Norgren, 1978b), which has been used extensively in assessing the interaction of taste processing and ingestive behaviors (Flynn, 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Stereotypic responses to controlled tastes have been found to be independent of cortical areas, and highly consistent across animals, suggesting that there may be a brainstem substrate for these behaviors.
claims.source: These stereotypic responses to controlled tastes have been found to be independent of cortical areas, and highly consistent across animals, suggesting that there may be a brainstem substrate for these behaviors (Grill and Norgren, 1978a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The direct innervation of tongue motoneurons by NTS neurons may be one neural substrate for taste reactivity behaviors.
claims.source: Our finding of a direct innervation of tongue motoneurons by NTS neurons may be one such neural substrate.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the anatomical data.

claims.claim: The DCN had not previously been implicated in directly contacting masseter or genioglossus motoneurons of the brainstem in the neonate.
claims.source: The DCN had not previously been implicated in directly contacting masseter or genioglossus motoneurons of the brainstem in the neonate.
claims.evidence: This statement identifies a gap in previous knowledge.

claims.claim: Where DCN axons project into the brainstem in non-murine species, the projection path is known to be primarily ipsilateral, with only sparse contralateral projections.
claims.source: Furthermore, where DCN axons project into the brainstem in non-murine species, the projection path is known to be primarily ipsilateral, with only sparse contralateral projections (Cohen et al., 1958; Ruigrok and Voogd, 1990).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Previous retrograde or transsynaptic tracing studies in rodents did not comment on any deep cerebellar nuclei labeling, even in polysynaptic tracing experiments.
claims.source: Previous retrograde or transsynaptic tracing studies in rodents did not comment on any deep cerebellar nuclei labeling, even in polysynaptic tracing experiments (Travers and Norgren, 1983; Fay and Norgren, 1997; Kolta et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The fastigial nucleus of the DCN provides inputs onto contralateral masseter motoneurons in the early postnatal mouse.
claims.source: By contrast, in our transsynaptic studies we found that the fastigial nucleus of the DCN provides inputs onto contralateral masseter motoneurons in the early postnatal mouse (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the tracing data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: A small number of neurons in both the fastigial and dentate nuclei of the DCN provide inputs onto genioglossus motoneurons.
claims.source: Additionally, we observed that a small number of neurons in both the fastigial and dentate nuclei of the DCN provide inputs onto genioglossus motoneurons (Figure 4D, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the tracing data shown in Figure 4D and Video 2.

claims.claim: Fastigial neurons give rise to a major contralateral projection pathway (as well as ipsilateral projections) and sparse fastigial axon terminals can be seen inside the contralateral MoV in adult mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, fastigial neurons give rise to a major contralateral projection pathway (as well as ipsilateral projections) and sparse fastigial axon terminals can be seen inside the contralateral MoV (Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas, 2014a; Oh, et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Allen Brain Connectivity Atlas.

claims.claim: Tracing results from either the fastigial or the dentate nucleus revealed sparse axon terminals inside MoXII in adult mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, tracing results from either the fastigial or the dentate nucleus revealed sparse axon terminals inside MoXII (Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas, 2014b; Oh, et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Allen Brain Connectivity Atlas.

claims.claim: It is possible that in newborn mice there are transiently more connections from DCN to MoV and MoXII.
claims.source: Although these DCN innervations of contralateral MoV and MoXII are sparse in adult mice, it is possible that in newborn mice there are transiently more connections.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on comparison of data from different developmental stages.

claims.claim: In P8→P15 masseter tracing experiment, no labeling in the DCN was observed.
claims.source: Notably, in our P8→P15 masseter tracing experiment, we did not observe any labeling in the DCN, supporting such transient projections from DCN to masseter and genioglossus motoneurons during early development.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the P8→P15 tracing experiments.

claims.claim: The absence of DCN labeling in P8→P15 tracing supports the hypothesis of transient projections from DCN to masseter and genioglossus motoneurons during early development.
claims.source: Notably, in our P8→P15 masseter tracing experiment, we did not observe any labeling in the DCN, supporting such transient projections from DCN to masseter and genioglossus motoneurons during early development.

results.result: The masseter premotor circuitry contains extensive bilateral populations in reticular nuclei (IRt, MdRt, PCRt), proprioceptive MesV neurons, sensory neurons in trigeminal nuclei (SpO, dPrV), neurons surrounding MoV, and descending inputs from DCN, dMRf, and RN.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C32 are well-supported by the rabies tracing data shown in Figure 2 and quantified in Table 1. The anatomical distribution is systematically documented across multiple brain regions with consistent labeling patterns across n=5 mice, providing robust evidence for the masseter premotor circuit organization.

results.result: The genioglossus premotor circuitry contains bilateral IRt/PCRt populations, sensory inputs from SpC/dPrV/MesV, taste-related NTS neurons, and descending inputs from DCN and dMRf.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 are supported by rabies tracing data in Figure 4 and Table 2 (n=5 mice). The systematic mapping reveals distinct sensory inputs compared to masseter, particularly the NTS taste-related input unique to genioglossus, providing clear anatomical evidence for the tongue premotor circuit.

results.result: Bilaterally projecting premotor neurons innervate both left and right masseter motoneurons, providing a mechanism for bilateral jaw coordination. Approximately 8% of premotor neurons were double-labeled, though this likely underestimates the true proportion.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C53 are supported by dual-color rabies tracing (Figure 3) and ChAT immunostaining showing GFP+ boutons contacting contralateral motoneurons. The authors appropriately acknowledge technical limitations (C52) that may cause underestimation. The anatomical evidence clearly demonstrates bilateral projections, though functional validation would strengthen the coordination claim.

results.result: Genioglossus premotor neurons send axon collaterals to digastric (jaw-opening) and central MoVII (platysma/lower lip) motoneurons, forming synaptic boutons that provide a mechanism for co-activation during tongue protrusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C69 are supported by anatomical tracing showing axon collaterals (Figures 4E, 4C, 5C) and high-resolution confocal microscopy demonstrating GFP+ boutons contacting ChAT+ motoneurons (Figure 5A-D). The anatomical connectivity is well-documented, though the functional interpretation (C69) as the 'simplest mechanism' is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: Masseter premotor axons innervate dorsal MoXII (tongue-retractor) motoneurons bilaterally, potentially facilitating co-activation of jaw-closing and tongue-retracting muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 5E-H) showing masseter premotor axons forming boutons on dorsal MoXII motoneurons. The anatomical evidence is clear, though the functional interpretation (C74) is inferential and would benefit from physiological validation.

results.result: Masseter and genioglossus motoneurons receive distinct sensory inputs: masseter receives MesV proprioceptive and SpVo somatosensory inputs, while genioglossus receives SpVc somatosensory and NTS taste inputs. Both receive dPrV inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C79 are supported by comparison of tracing data from Figures 2 and 4, Tables 1 and 2. The differential sensory innervation patterns are clearly documented and quantified, providing strong evidence for distinct sensory processing streams for jaw versus tongue control.

results.result: Masseter and genioglossus premotor neurons are spatially intermixed in rostral IRt/PCRt regions containing CPG circuitry, but remain distinct populations with no double-labeled neurons, preventing simultaneous activation that could cause tongue-biting.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C86 are supported by dual-color tracing (Figure 6) showing spatial overlap without double-labeling. The anatomical segregation is well-documented, and the functional interpretation (C86) regarding tongue-biting prevention is logical. The connection to CPG regions (C84) is supported by citations to prior work.

results.result: Premotor neurons in IRt have mixed neurotransmitter phenotypes (excitatory vGluT2+, inhibitory GAD1/2+ or GlyT2+), while DCN and dMRf neurons are exclusively excitatory (vGluT2+), suggesting descending inputs are primarily excitatory.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 7). The mixed phenotypes in IRt and exclusive glutamatergic phenotype in DCN/dMRf are clearly demonstrated. However, the authors note they could not reliably quantify percentages due to viral toxicity, which is an appropriate limitation to acknowledge.

results.result: P8→P15 tracing showed reduced motoneuron infection efficiency and overall premotor labeling compared to P1→P8, but similar distribution patterns. LPGi neurons showed increased labeling when normalized to motoneuron numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 are supported by quantitative data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The developmental comparison is appropriately controlled by normalizing to motoneuron infection. The increased LPGi connectivity suggests developmental changes, though the reduced overall efficiency limits broader conclusions about circuit maturation.

results.result: DCN (fastigial nucleus) provides contralateral inputs to masseter motoneurons and bilateral inputs to genioglossus motoneurons in neonatal mice. These connections may be transient, as P8→P15 tracing showed no DCN labeling and adult Allen Brain Atlas data shows only sparse terminals.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C133 are supported by P1→P8 tracing data (Figures 2C, 4D) and comparison with P8→P15 data and Allen Brain Atlas. The developmental comparison strengthens the transient connection hypothesis (C133), though this remains inferential. The finding is novel and appropriately contextualized with existing literature.

results.result: A few bilaterally projecting MesV primary afferent neurons were observed in P1→P8 tracing but not in P8→P15 tracing, suggesting these may be transient developmental connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C136 are based on very sparse observations ('very few' C134) with developmental comparison. While the P8→P15 data supports the transient hypothesis, the extremely low numbers and lack of quantification make this finding uncertain. This could represent biological variability or technical artifact rather than a true developmental phenomenon.

results.result: P1→P8 masseter premotor circuits likely reflect suckling control, as chewing emerges around P12. The same circuitry may be reused for chewing after glycine switches from excitatory to inhibitory signaling during development.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 are speculative interpretations based on developmental timing (C34, supported by citation) and prior work on glycine signaling (C35). However, the study does not directly test whether the P1→P8 circuits control suckling or whether they are reused for chewing. The hypothesis (C36) is reasonable but requires functional validation.

results.result: NTS neurons provide monosynaptic input to genioglossus motoneurons, potentially serving as a brainstem substrate for taste reactivity behaviors that are independent of cortical areas.
results.evaluation: Claim C120 is directly supported by tracing data (Figure 4B). Claims C121-C122 are supported by citations to prior behavioral work. The interpretation (C123) that this connection underlies taste reactivity is reasonable given the anatomical evidence and prior literature, though functional testing would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: The jaw premotor circuit includes bilaterally projecting neurons that synapse on equivalent ipsilateral and contralateral motoneurons, representing the simplest configuration for bilateral coordination. These neurons are especially prevalent in the reticular formation region containing the jaw CPG.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are supported by anatomical data (Figures 3, 6) and citations to prior CPG localization studies. The 'simplest configuration' interpretation (C99) is reasonable given the anatomical evidence, though alternative mechanisms are not ruled out. The prevalence in CPG regions (C100) is well-documented.

results.result: Shared premotor neurons simultaneously innervating multiple motoneuron groups provide the simplest mechanism for orofacial muscle co-activation and may represent a common circuit mechanism for motor coordination. These are likely located in IRt where most premotor neurons reside.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 are supported by the anatomical data showing multi-target premotor neurons (Figures 4, 5). The generalization (C137) is reasonable but extends beyond the data. The 'simplest mechanism' interpretation is logical given the anatomy, though functional validation and comparison with alternative mechanisms would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Masseter and genioglossus premotor neurons are spatially intermixed in the region containing the chewing CPG. Combined with prior intracellular recordings showing masseter receives rhythmic inhibitory and excitatory signals while genioglossus receives only excitatory signals, and current data showing mixed transmitter phenotypes, this suggests premotor neurons for different muscles are embedded within the same rhythm-generating network.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 integrate current anatomical data (Figure 6C, Figure 7) with prior electrophysiological work (C115-C116, supported by citations) and CPG localization (C113, supported by citations). The synthesis (C114) is a reasonable inference, though direct functional testing of the proposed network interactions would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Only 1-3 ChAT+ premotor neurons were labeled in reticular regions, with inconsistent rostral-caudal positioning across samples, suggesting secondary viral jumping from these neurons would be very sparse and inconsistent.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C143 are supported by immunostaining data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This addresses an important methodological concern about potential multi-synaptic labeling. The low and inconsistent labeling appropriately justifies focusing analysis on consistently labeled regions, though it doesn't completely rule out some secondary jumping.

results.result: Feeding behaviors require coordinated activation of jaw, tongue, and face muscles, with three basic forms of coordination: bilateral jaw symmetry, similar rhythm for tongue and jaw, and co-activation of tongue-protruding/jaw-opening versus tongue-retracting/jaw-closing muscles. The neural substrates for this coordination remain unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C16 establish the behavioral context and knowledge gap. These are well-supported by multiple citations to prior behavioral studies (C7, C10-C16). Claims C1-C2 appropriately frame the study's motivation. This background is essential for interpreting the anatomical findings but represents prior knowledge rather than new results.

results.result: In spinal locomotor circuits, separate CPGs control separate limb muscles with coordination occurring through CPG interactions. By analogy, orofacial muscles might use similar mechanisms, though evidence for well-defined jaw, face, and tongue CPGs is lacking. Previous studies suggest neurons projecting to multiple cranial motor nuclei exist.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21 provide theoretical context from spinal cord literature (C17-C19, supported by citations) and identify the knowledge gap for orofacial circuits (C20). Claim C21 is supported by citations to prior anatomical work. This appropriately frames the study's contribution but represents background rather than new findings.

results.result: The monosynaptic rabies virus method used is deficient for rabies-G, preventing spread beyond directly presynaptic neurons, and infects neurons irrespective of neurotransmitter phenotype, size, or morphology, enabling unbiased assessment.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C139 describe the methodological approach and are supported by citations to prior methods papers. This is essential methodological information that validates the tracing strategy. The claims accurately represent the properties of the rabies tracing system as established in the cited literature.
